passages.happening:
Nicodemus is a Pharisee and ‘a leader of the Jews’. He comes to Jesus at night and says, “Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God” (verse 2). No one could do such signs, he says, unless God were with him.

Jesus answers something Nicodemus did not ask: “no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again” (verse 3). Nicodemus is puzzled. How can a grown man be born? Can he go back into his mother's womb? Jesus says it again, more fully: “no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit” (verse 5). Flesh gives birth to flesh, and the Spirit gives birth to spirit.

Do not be amazed, Jesus says. The wind blows wherever it wants. You hear it, but you cannot tell where it comes from or where it is going. “So it is with everyone born of the Spirit” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The Pharisees were a movement of devout Jews who tried to keep God's law carefully in everyday life, and the people respected them. Nicodemus is also a leader. Later he is found among the chief priests and Pharisees, asking that Jesus be given a fair hearing (7:45-51). He is the most religious man in the room, and he is the first person in John to be told he must be born anew.

Why does he come at night? Perhaps he did not want to be seen. Perhaps night was simply a quiet time for long talk. John does not say. But John has already said that the light shines in the darkness (1:5), and the reader notices a man coming out of the night toward the light.

The key word in verse 3 is anōthen. It means both ‘again’ and ‘from above’. Nicodemus hears ‘again’: a second birth from a mother. Jesus means ‘from above’: a birth that comes from God. In verse 31 the same word plainly means ‘from above’. Many readers think John means both: a second birth, whose source is heaven. That is why some Bibles say ‘born again’ and others ‘born from above’.

In verse 8 Jesus plays on another word. In Greek, as in Hebrew, one word means both ‘wind’ and ‘spirit’. You cannot see the wind or steer it. You can only see what it does. So it is with the Spirit's work in a person.
passages.ot: Jesus expects Nicodemus to know this already: ‘You are Israel's teacher, and you do not understand these things?’ (verse 10). The prophets had promised it. Through Ezekiel God said, “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean”, and “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:25-26). Water and Spirit, side by side, for a people made new. In the next chapter of Ezekiel, God's breath comes into a valley of dry bones, “so that they may live” (Ezekiel 37:9).
passages.hard:
What does ‘born of water and the Spirit’ mean? Christians read it in three main ways, and each has careful defenders.

Baptism. From early times many Christians have read the water as baptism. John has just told of John the Baptist baptizing with water (1:26-33), and later in this chapter Jesus' disciples are baptizing (verse 22). Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and many Anglican Christians hold that God gives the new birth through baptism, joined to faith. Paul speaks of “the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).

The cleansing Ezekiel promised. Others read water and Spirit as one thing: the cleansing and renewing God promised in Ezekiel 36, which Israel's teacher should have known (verse 10). John Calvin read it this way. On this view Jesus is pointing to the promise, before Christian baptism began.

Natural birth, then the new birth. Others think ‘water’ means ordinary human birth, and ‘Spirit’ the second birth from God, since verse 6 sets flesh beside Spirit.

These notes do not choose. Christians who differ here agree on more than they disagree. No one enters God's kingdom by effort or by family line, and the new birth is the Spirit's work.
passages.asks: Nicodemus came with a compliment and was told he needed a new start. That can sting. Being respected, careful and devout is good, but it is not the same as new life from God. No one can give birth to himself. Have you been trying to improve the old life, when what is offered is a new one?

passages.t: As Moses lifted up the snake
passages.happening:
“How can this be?” Nicodemus asks (verse 9). Jesus answers that Israel's teacher ought to understand. He speaks of what he knows and has seen, and still people do not accept it. If they do not believe him about earthly things, how will they believe him about heavenly things? No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven: the Son of Man (verse 13).

Then Jesus gives a picture from Israel's years in the wilderness. “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life” (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
‘Lifted up’ has two meanings, and John wants both. It can mean raised high in honour. It can also mean raised up on a pole or a cross. Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves and rebels, carried out in public where everyone could see. Later John explains that Jesus spoke of being lifted up “to indicate the kind of death He was going to die” (12:33). The cross, the shameful pole, is where the Son is raised high.

‘Eternal life’ appears here for the first time in John. It means the life of the age to come, God's own life, given now to the one who believes, and never ending.

Notice the word ‘must’ in verse 14. It is the same word as in ‘you must be born again’ (verse 7). Both the new birth and the cross are part of God's plan, not accidents.
passages.ot:
The story is in Numbers 21:4-9. In the wilderness the people complained against God and Moses. Venomous snakes came among them, and many died. When they asked for help, God told Moses to make a snake and set it on a pole: “When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live” (Numbers 21:8). Moses made it of bronze, and those who looked lived.

Jewish teachers were careful to say that the bronze snake itself did not heal. The Wisdom of Solomon, a Jewish book written in Greek, probably before Jesus' time, says the one who turned toward it was saved not by what he saw, but by God, the Saviour of all (16:7). The Mishnah, written down later, says Israel was healed when they looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven (Rosh Hashanah 3:8). Centuries after Moses the bronze snake had become an idol, and King Hezekiah broke it up (2 Kings 18:4).

Jesus takes up the old story. The people were dying from a poison they had brought on themselves. God provided the cure. It was lifted up where all could see it. And it worked by looking, not by doing.
passages.asks: The Israelites were not healed by understanding how the bronze snake worked. They were healed by looking at what God had lifted up. You do not need to understand everything before you look to Jesus. What would it mean for you to stop staring at your own wounds, and look to him?

passages.happening:
Now comes perhaps the best-known verse in the Bible: “For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life” (verse 16). God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through him (verse 17).

Whoever believes in him is not condemned. Whoever does not believe stands condemned already, because he has not believed in God's one and only Son (verse 18). This is the verdict: the light has come into the world, but people loved the darkness rather than the light, because what they did was evil. Whoever does evil hates the light and stays away from it, so that his deeds will not be exposed. But whoever practises the truth comes into the light (verses 19-21).
passages.hearers:
‘So loved’ can mean ‘loved so much’, but the Greek word's usual meaning is ‘loved in this way’. Many scholars think John means both: how much God loved, and how he showed it. The ‘way’ points back to verse 14. God loved the world by giving his Son to be lifted up.

‘The world’ in John often means people turned away from God, the world that did not know its own maker (1:10). That is what makes the verse astonishing. God loves the world not because it is lovable, but while it is set against him.

‘One and only’ translates a Greek word that means ‘unique, the only one of his kind’. Older Bibles said ‘only begotten’. Either way, Jesus is God's Son as no one else is.

The old Greek copies had no quotation marks, so editors must decide where Jesus' words end. Some end them at verse 15 and hear John himself speaking from verse 16. Most Bibles, the Berean Standard Bible among them, run Jesus' words to verse 21. The meaning does not change.
passages.ot: Many readers hear behind ‘gave His one and only Son’ the story of Abraham, to whom God said, “Take your son,” and then, “your only son Isaac, whom you love” (Genesis 22:2). Abraham's son was spared, and a ram was given in his place. God's own Son was not spared. Paul puts it this way: “He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).
passages.hard:
Verse 18 says that whoever does not believe ‘has already been condemned’. Does that mean God is eager to condemn? Read it slowly. Verse 17 says the Son did not come to condemn but to save. The verdict in verse 19 is not a new sentence passed on people. It describes what is already true when people turn from the light. Jesus comes as a rescuer into a world already in the dark.

These are serious words. They are not meant to frighten anyone into faith. They are meant to show how much is offered. If you are unsure where you stand, the verse does not tell you to stare at your fear. It points you to the Son God gave.

Christians also ask about people who never heard of Jesus. This passage speaks to those who have met the light, and it does not answer that question. Faithful Christians have held different views on it.
passages.asks: John 3:16 is so familiar that it can sound like a slogan. Read it as if for the first time: God, who owes the world nothing, gives what is most precious to him for people who did not want him. Where do you still act as if God's love must be earned? And what in you would rather stay in the dark than be seen?

passages.happening:
After this, Jesus and his disciples go out into the Judean countryside, where he spends time with them and baptizes. John the Baptist is baptizing too, at Aenon near Salim, because there is plenty of water there (verse 23). John has not yet been put in prison.

An argument starts between John's disciples and a certain Jew about ceremonial washing. Then John's disciples come to him, worried. The man you pointed to, they say, is baptizing, ‘and everyone is going to Him’ (verse 26).

John is not worried at all. A man can receive only what is given him from heaven. He reminds them that he said he was not the Christ. The bride belongs to the groom. The groom's friend stands and listens for him, and is full of joy when he hears the groom's voice. “That joy is mine, and it is now complete,” John says. “He must increase; I must decrease” (verses 29-30).
passages.hearers:
John adds a little later that Jesus himself did not baptize; his disciples did (4:2).

Aenon near Salim cannot be placed with certainty. A fourth-century list of Bible places by Eusebius puts it eight Roman miles south of Scythopolis, in the Jordan valley. Others look for it in Samaria, near springs east of Shechem. No site has been confirmed.

The note about prison assumes that readers knew John was later arrested by Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, and killed (Mark 6:17-29). It also helps fit John's story with Mark's, where Jesus begins preaching in Galilee “After the arrest of John” (Mark 1:14). Only John tells of this earlier time, when the two baptized side by side.

The ‘friend of the bridegroom’ was the groom's close friend at the wedding. His joy was to see the groom and his bride together. He would never try to win the bride for himself.
passages.ot: The prophets often speak of God as Israel's husband: “I will betroth you to Me forever” (Hosea 2:19), and “as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). So when John calls Jesus the bridegroom, he gives him a place the Old Testament gave to God himself. John is only the friend who brought the bride.
passages.hard: Does ‘I must decrease’ mean that Christians should despise themselves? No. John is not sad. He says his joy is complete. He is like the best man at a wedding, glad to step back so that the groom can be seen. Making much of Christ does not mean making nothing of yourself. It means being glad when he is the one people see.
passages.asks: John's disciples were jealous for him. John was not. He knew what was his and what was not, and he found his joy in someone else's increase. Where are you comparing yourself with someone whose work is growing while yours shrinks? What would it take for their increase to become your joy?

passages.t: The one who comes from above
passages.happening:
The one who comes from above is above all, the chapter goes on. The one who is from the earth speaks as one from the earth. The one from heaven tells what he has seen and heard, yet few accept it. Whoever does accept it “has certified that God is truthful” (verse 33). The one God has sent speaks God's words, for God gives the Spirit without limit (verse 34). The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands.

The chapter ends: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life. Instead, the wrath of God remains on him” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
These verses may be John the Baptist still speaking, or the writer reflecting on what he said. Bibles differ on where the quotation marks go.

‘From above’ is the same word as in verse 3, anōthen. Now its meaning is plain: Jesus comes from God.

‘Certified’ translates a Greek word meaning ‘set one's seal on’, the way a witness pressed his seal on a document to say that it was true. To believe Jesus is to put your seal on God's truthfulness.

‘Rejects’ is a strong word. In Greek it means ‘refuses to obey’. It does not describe someone who has never heard, or someone who is still asking questions. And ‘remains’ means that God's anger is not newly thrown at the person. It stays where it already was, because the one who came to lift it was turned away.
passages.ot: God's anger in the Bible is not a bad temper. It is his steady opposition to evil, the anger of a good judge against what destroys people. A psalm says, “God is a righteous judge” (Psalm 7:11). Another says, “He has not dealt with us according to our sins” (Psalm 103:10). This chapter holds both. God's anger against evil is real, and God's love has given the Son so that no one need stay under it.
passages.hard:
Is verse 36 meant to scare people? It is meant to be honest. The same chapter says that God loved the world (verse 16) and sent his Son not to condemn but to save (verse 17). The wrath ‘remains’ only where the Son is refused. Judgment belongs to God, who knows each heart. Someone troubled by these words is usually still listening, and listening is where believing begins.

If you are grieving someone who died without clear faith, these verses may hurt. This passage does not tell us what passed between that person and God at the end. It does tell us who the judge is: the same Jesus who spent a whole night patiently with a slow and puzzled man.
passages.asks: This chapter began with a man who came at night with questions, and it ends with a choice: to believe the Son, or to refuse him. Nicodemus did not decide that night. John follows him later, speaking up for Jesus (7:50-51) and helping to bury him (19:39). If you are somewhere between the night and the light, you are in good company. Keep coming.
